title: Measuring a studio blog by conversations
metaTitle: Measure a studio blog by conversations
excerpt: Count a qualified conversation: the right buyer, from a page that answered their question. Sessions are context, not the result.
alt: A pale room with an arched opening onto a dark sofa, a low table, and a glass vase of dried stems, a quiet place where a real conversation could start.
caption: A pale room opening onto a sofa and a low table. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a studio count from its blog?
faqs.answer: Count qualified conversations: the right buyer, who read a page that answered their question, and then wrote or booked a call. Sessions, rankings, and time on page are context for that number. A busy page that attracts the wrong people is not a success.

faqs.question: Are sessions useless?
faqs.answer: Sessions tell you whether anyone arrived and which URL they landed on, and they become misleading when they are treated as the goal. A dump of thin posts can raise sessions and lower the number of serious conversations. Read sessions beside the conversations, not instead of them.

faqs.question: How do we know which page earned the conversation?
faqs.answer: Ask which piece they read, on the intro call and in the inbox, and keep the answer. A short monthly list of URL plus who wrote is enough. You do not need a large attribution model to see which essays are doing the job.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Content marketing leads, for a studio, are not a spike in sessions. The number that matters is a qualified conversation: the right buyer, from a page that answered their question. Sessions are context. They tell you the piece was found. They do not tell you it did its job.

If you only watch traffic, you will publish whatever moves the chart. The chart is the wrong client.

## The conversation is the result

A qualified conversation has three parts. The person could actually hire you, or they influence the person who could. They can point at a page, or at a problem the page was about. And they are talking about the work, not asking you to explain a headline that never landed.

That is a high bar on purpose. A student writing a paper, a recruiter, and a competitor skimming your process are all "engagement." They are not the result the studio is publishing for. Be polite to them. Do not build the next quarter's plan around them. The plan should ask which pages a founder mentioned when they booked time, and which pages were open when a serious email arrived.

Write the definition down so it survives a good month. When sessions jump, someone will want to call the jump a win. The definition keeps you honest. A win is a conversation you would want again, with a person who understood the offer well enough to ask a specific question. "I read the piece on what to keep in a redesign" is a win. "I saw you rank for design" is not yet anything.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether someone leaves having learned enough to achieve a goal, and whether you would expect the page to be recommended. A conversation is that test with a name attached. The reader achieved a goal: they decided to talk. If your pages are recommended only inside analytics, and never by a person, you have not finished the job. The guidance also warns against producing lots of pages in the hope that some of them perform. Performance, here, has to mean the conversation. Otherwise "perform" will quietly turn into "attract a visit."

## What "qualified" excludes

Exclude vanity that feels like interest. A newsletter signup with no context is not a conversation. A like is not a conversation. A long session from your own team, checking the deploy, is not a conversation. A form filled by someone who wants a price in the next ten minutes, and who has not read anything, is a conversation of a sort, and it is usually a bad one. Note it separately so it does not flatter the page.

Include the quiet ones. A founder who replies to a short email and names the essay. A referral who says "they sent me the article about the first screen." A past client who forwards a piece to a colleague because it describes the work you did together, without inventing a quote. Those rarely show up as goals in a dashboard. They show up in the inbox and on the call. If your measurement never looks there, it will prefer the pages that attract wanderers.

The right buyer for Hanabi is a founder or a small team lead who needs a site, a brand that can survive contact with the interface, or a product surface designed and built with care. Public proof sits in projects like Down the Cove, Thomas Bewick, Ballarat Box Sports, Wabisabi, Got Next, Leadly, and Trade Moai. A conversation that is about that kind of work is qualified. A conversation that wants a cheap template by Friday is information about your headlines, not a lead to celebrate.

## Sessions are context

Keep the session count. Use it as a denominator and a warning light, not as a trophy. Which URLs were entered? Did the newest piece get any visits at all? Did a dump of posts raise traffic and flatten replies? That last pattern is common, and it is the argument against publishing a hundred thin pages in a day. The chart goes up. The inbox does not get more serious.

Time on page is a weaker signal than it looks. [Nielsen Norman Group's summary of the research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is blunt: people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, the average visit is under a minute, and the average hides the real shape. Most pages are judged quickly and abandoned. The ones that state a clear value early are the ones that sometimes earn minutes. A "high average time" can be a few patient readers and a crowd who left immediately, averaged into a number that looks fine. Do not pay yourself for it.

Use the 10-second finding as a writing constraint, not as a KPI to game. The first paragraphs have to say the answer, because many readers will not stay long enough for a warm-up. If the right buyers are bouncing, the opening is wrong or the query that brought them was. If the wrong buyers are staying for minutes, you may have written a general essay that is interesting and unspecific. Interesting is not the goal. A conversation with the right person is.

Rankings belong in the same drawer as sessions. A page on the first page for a phrase you do not want to be hired for is a cost. It attracts the wrong conversations, and those conversations train you to sound like the phrase. Check the queries that lead to real calls. Let the others be context.

## A monthly note, not a dashboard religion

Once a month, write a short note. How many qualified conversations. Which URLs were named. What the person already understood, and what they still needed. What you will change: a paragraph, a link, a page you will stop promoting, a page you owe the archive because the same question keeps arriving without a good answer.

Five lines beat a quarterly slide. The note should be boring enough to keep. "Two conversations. One from the redesign piece, a founder with a live store. One from the author page, a referral. Nothing from the three posts we published to cover synonyms. Next month, no more synonym posts. Update the redesign piece, the tool it mentions has changed." That note will improve the site more than a funnel chart.

Do not invent a revenue number the blog "generated." A studio that attributes a project to a single article is usually telling a story after the fact. You can say the article started the conversation. You cannot honestly put a price on the essay unless the commercial path is that simple, and it rarely is. Leave the fiction out of the report. Clients can feel it when a studio's own marketing math is decorative.

If a month has zero conversations, say zero. Then ask whether nobody came, or people came and the page gave them no next step, or the next step was wrong. Those are different repairs. The first is distribution and the query. The second is the ending of the piece. The third is the offer. Mixing them up is how a team "fixes" a good essay by adding a louder button.

## Which pages earn their place

After a few notes, patterns show up. The pages that earn conversations are usually the ones that take a side: what to keep in a rebuild, what a first screen must show, what you should own in the repository. The pages that earn sessions and no conversations are usually the definitions, the glossaries, and the lists of trends. Keep a definition if other pages rely on it. Do not keep a trend piece because it once spiked.

Look at the path, not only the landing URL. A buyer may land on a narrow answer, click to the piece about how you work, and only then write. The narrow answer still mattered. Credit it. A buyer may land on the homepage from memory and never touch the blog. The blog did not fail that month. It was not in the path. Your note should allow both facts.

Retire pages that create the wrong conversations. A page that ranks for cheap, fast, no-process work will fill the calendar with calls you will decline. Unpublishing it feels like losing traffic. It is losing the wrong traffic. Redirect it to the page that says who the work is for, if that page exists. If the honest answer is "not us," a short page that says so will save everyone an hour.

[Selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) is the other measure sitting next to the essay. Conversations that reference a project are further along than conversations that reference only a concept. When the writing and the work point at the same kind of problem, the call starts in the middle, which is where you want it.

## What not to optimize

Do not optimize the subject line of the studio's personality. A more aggressive excerpt can raise clicks and lower trust. Nielsen's point about the first seconds applies to the search result too: people decide quickly whether the page is for them. A stuffed line attracts the click and fails the second test, on the page. You will see the session. You will not see the person who almost wrote and then did not.

Do not add popups to "capture" the visit you were about to waste. A founder who was ready to talk can use a link. A founder who was not ready will not become ready because a modal interrupted the answer. Finish the answer. Offer the next step once, in a sentence.

Do not pay for more traffic to a page that does not convert the right reader. You will learn nothing except that more of the wrong people can be bought. Fix the page, or accept that this topic is a public service and not a source of work. Both are allowed. Only one of them should be in the lead count.

## How the page asks for the conversation

The ending of the essay is part of the measurement. If you never say what to do next, you will undercount interest, because interest had nowhere to go. If you say it in a way that ignores the article, you will attract people who did not read it. Match the ask to the piece. Proof points at the work. A hiring question points at a call. A technical repair points at the service that includes the repair.

Track the ask simply. A dedicated link is enough to see whether anyone used it. Then compare that click to the conversations, because a click is still not a conversation. The monthly note should mention both, and trust the second.

When the same question shows up in three conversations and the page that should answer it is out of date, the next job is not another new URL. [Updating a post when the answer changes](/blog/updating-a-post-when-the-answer-changes) is the next piece, because a page that already earns trust will lose it the moment the advice goes stale.
